fuller.text: This short 2009 essay by Paul Graham asks why talk about politics and religion goes so badly. He notes that online forums slide into religious arguments far more than into fights about Javascript or baking. His first clue is that people feel no expertise is needed to have opinions on religion, only strong beliefs.

sentences.text: This short 2009 essay by Paul Graham asks why talk about politics and religion goes so badly.
He notes that online forums slide into religious arguments far more than into fights about Javascript or baking.
His first clue is that people feel no expertise is needed to have opinions on religion, only strong beliefs.

fuller.text: He tests one explanation and rejects it: that these topics have no definite answers, so no one can be proven wrong. Some political questions do have answers, like what a new policy will cost, yet they go just as badly. His answer instead is identity: people cannot argue usefully about something that has become part of who they are.

fuller.text: He backs this with examples showing the trouble depends on the people, not the topic. A battle involving your own country starts a fight, but a Bronze Age battle does not, since no one knows which side to take. Programming languages spark "religious wars" because coders see themselves as X or Y programmers, yet languages can still be better or worse designed. Even Ford versus Chevy trucks can be unsafe to discuss with some people.

fuller.text: He hedges that the theory may be wrong, but if right, it also shows how to think better. Since people cannot think clearly about parts of their identity, the best plan is to let as few things in as possible. He allows exceptions like being a scientist, which commits you only to following the evidence. His conclusion: the more labels you have for yourself, the dumber they make you.

brief.text: In this short essay, Paul Graham asks why online talk about politics and religion goes so badly. People argue about them far more than about topics like baking, with no expert knowledge needed. His answer is that these topics become part of people's identity: who they feel they are.

brief.text: What causes trouble depends on the people, not the topic. Even programming languages or pickup trucks can spark fights if people tie them to who they are. If his idea is right, it also shows how to think more clearly. Let as few things as possible into your identity, because labels for yourself make you think worse.
